title: RCMP to probe man's death four days after Taser use
article: Before deploying a Taser, pepper spray and a baton on a 36-year-old Chilliwack man who died in hospital this weekend, police tried to physically restrain him, an RCMP spokesperson said Sunday.
"First was an attempt at physical restraint which failed," said Const. Lea-Anne Dunlop of a Nov. 19 police confrontation with Robert Knipstrom in Chilliwack.
"That didn't work, and he was pepper sprayed, and subsequently the Taser was introduced as was the baton," Dunlop said.

Knipstrom's death is being investigated as an in-custody death by the RCMP major crime section in conjunction with the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team, Abbotsford Police and the Vancouver Island Major Crime Unit, Dunlop said.

She added that due to the high-profile nature of the case, "an observer from the commission of public complaints has been monitoring the investigation from the beginning with full and unfettered access."
The investigation will focus on whether the use of force by officers was in line with police protocol and the Criminal Code.
The involvement of the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team is standard procedure with in-custody deaths, Dunlop said.
A coroner's investigation is also underway, and has yet to determine whether Knipstrom was on drugs at the time of the incident or if the Taser actually made contact with him, Dunlop said.

Knipstrom had been seen driving dangerously through Chilliwack streets before he entered the Eze Rent-It Centre. When police arrived, they said they found Knipstrom acting agitated and erratic. When he died in hospital Saturday, he became the third fatality following police use of Tasers in Canada in six weeks.

On Nov. 22, 45-year-old Howard Hyde died in a Dartmouth, N.S., prison after police deployed a Taser. Since the death of Robert Dziekanski at the Vancouver Airport Oct. 14, a public outcry over police use of the conducted energy weapons has been mounting. More than 1,000 people reportedly participated in a rally at the Vancouver Art Gallery Saturday in memory of Dziekanski, one of three held across Canada.
Donna Sitter, a spokesperson for Solicitor General John Les, said Sunday that the minister is not considering a moratorium on the use of Tasers at this time.
Dunlop acknowledged that Tasers are "a sensitive issue right now," but, she said, Chilliwack police will continue to use the weapons.

"They are an intervention option that is utilized for combative subjects," she said. "They fall in line on our intervention model in the same area where pepper spray and our baton would fall as well."
Meanwhile, the Canada Border Services Agency has announced they will release an internal report Monday on the events surrounding Dziekanski's death.

CBSA spokesperson Paula Shore said the report will include recommendations for change, and will shed light on the hours Dziekanski spent in a secure area of the airport before the fatal confrontation with police.
